section.title: Job Answers Again
section.sectionRationale: Job answers Eliphaz's second speech with his sharpest description yet of feeling personally assaulted by God, pierced, torn, and surrounded like a target for archers. Yet in the middle of this darkest language, he reaches for one of the book's brightest flashes of hope: a witness in heaven, an advocate on high, someone who will plead for him with God as a man pleads for his neighbor.
section.thesis: Job's grief deepens into a vivid sense of divine assault, yet even here he does not abandon hope entirely, reaching instead for the conviction that a witness in heaven already sees his innocence and will one day plead his case.
section.frameNote: Five movements: Job's renewed rebuke of his friends as miserable comforters; his vivid, almost violent description of feeling torn and targeted by God Himself; his sudden flash of hope in a witness and advocate already in heaven; his continued lament over mockers who surround him and his broken spirit; and his closing questions about where any hope could possibly remain if Sheol is his only home.

units.label: Miserable comforters are you all
units.note: I could also speak like you

verses.text: Then Job answered:
"I have heard many things like these; miserable comforters are you all.
Is there no end to your long-winded speeches? What provokes you to continue testifying?
I could also speak like you if you were in my place; I could heap up words against you and shake my head at you.
But I would encourage you with my mouth, and the consolation of my lips would bring relief.

units.label: God has torn me
units.note: He has set me up as His target

verses.text: "Even if I speak, my pain is not relieved, and if I hold back, how will it go away?
Surely He has now exhausted me; You have devastated all my family.
You have bound me, and it has become a witness; my frailty rises up and testifies against me.

His anger has torn me and opposed me; He gnashes His teeth at me. 
My adversary pierces me with His eyes.

They open their mouths against me and strike my cheeks with contempt; 
they join together against me.
God has delivered me to unjust men; He has thrown me to the clutches of the wicked.
I was at ease, but He shattered me; He seized me by the neck and crushed me. He has set me up as His target;
His archers surround me. He pierces my kidneys without mercy and spills my gall on the ground.
He breaks me with wound upon wound; He rushes me like a mighty warrior.
I have sewn sackcloth over my skin; I have buried my horn in the dust.
My face is red with weeping, and deep shadows ring my eyes;
yet my hands are free of violence and my prayer is pure.
"O earth, do not cover my {{dam|blood}}; may my cry for help never be laid to rest.
Even now my {{ed|witness}} is in heaven, and my {{sahed|advocate}} is on high.
My friends are my scoffers as my eyes pour out tears to God.
Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!
For when only a few years are past I will go the way of no return.

units.label: My spirit is broken
units.note: the innocent are stirred against the godless

verses.text: "My spirit is broken; my days are extinguished; the grave awaits me.
Surely mockers surround me, and my eyes must gaze at their rebellion.
Give me, I pray, the pledge You demand. Who else will be my guarantor?
You have closed their minds to understanding; therefore You will not exalt them.
If a man denounces his friends for a price, the eyes of his children will fail.
He has made me a byword among the people, a man in whose face they spit.
My eyes have grown dim with grief, and my whole body is but a shadow.
The upright are appalled at this, and the innocent are stirred against the godless.
Yet a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger.

units.label: Where then is my hope?
units.note: will we go down together into the dust

verses.text: "But come back and try again, all of you. For I will not find a wise man among you.
My days have passed; my plans are broken off, even the desires of my heart.
They have turned night into day, making light seem near in the face of darkness.
If I look for Sheol as my home, if I spread out my bed in darkness,
and say to corruption, 'You are my father,' and to the worm, 'My mother,' or 'My sister,'
where then is my {{tiqvah|hope}}? Who can see any hope for me?
Will it go down to the gates of Sheol? Will we go down together into the dust?"

dam.gloss: Blood, life. Job's cry, do not cover my blood, echoes the blood of Abel crying out from the ground in Genesis 4:10, a plea that his suffering not be silenced or forgotten but heard as a genuine cry for justice.

ed.gloss: A witness, one who testifies to the truth of a matter. Job's declaration that his witness is in heaven marks a striking turn: even while feeling personally torn apart by God, he trusts that heaven itself holds testimony to his innocence.

sahed.gloss: An advocate or witness, a rare term, possibly an Aramaic loanword, appearing only here in the Old Testament. Paired with ed in the same verse, it intensifies Job's flash of hope: not just one witness but an advocate actively representing his case on high.

tiqvah.gloss: Hope, expectation. Job's repeated, aching question, where then is my hope, closes this speech on a note of apparent despair, yet the very fact that he keeps asking the question, rather than abandoning it, shows hope has not entirely died even here.

basic.context: Job again rebukes his friends as miserable comforters before describing, in his most violent language yet, how he feels personally targeted and torn apart by God, like a man shot at by archers or seized by the throat. Yet right at this darkest point, Job reaches for a sudden, striking hope: a witness in heaven and an advocate on high, someone who already knows the truth of his case and might one day plead it as a man pleads for his neighbor. He returns to lament, surrounded by mockers, his spirit broken, and closes by asking where any hope could remain if Sheol, the grave, is truly his only future.
basic.hermeneutics: This passage models the coexistence of despair and hope within a single, honest prayer. Job does not resolve his anguish before reaching for hope; the hope simply appears, briefly, in the middle of his darkest language, and then the darkness returns. This pattern, hope interrupting grief without fully dispelling it, is itself an important lesson for readers who expect faith to move in a straight line from despair to certainty.
basic.originalLanguages: Job cries that the earth not cover his dam, blood, echoing Abel's blood crying from the ground, and declares that his ed, witness, and sahed, advocate, a rare word found nowhere else in the Old Testament, are already in heaven. His closing question, where then is my tiqvah, hope, leaves the ache open rather than resolved, though the very act of asking shows hope persisting even in apparent despair.
basic.typology: Job's cry for a witness and advocate in heaven who could plead his case anticipates the New Testament's doctrine of Christ's heavenly intercession for His people, and his plea that the earth not cover his blood anticipates the greater blood of Christ, which, unlike Abel's, speaks a better word, not for vengeance but for mercy.
basic.christ: Job longs for a witness in heaven and an advocate on high, a role the New Testament reveals is filled by Christ Himself, who ever lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him. Job's cry that his blood not be covered but heard finds its ultimate answer in the blood of Christ, which speaks a better word than the blood of Abel, not crying for vengeance but securing mercy for all who trust in Him.
basic.god: God is experienced here as simultaneously assailant and hoped-for advocate, a tension the chapter does not resolve. Job does not abandon belief that God's own heaven holds a true witness to his case, even while he describes God's own hand as the source of his most violent suffering, holding together an honesty about pain and a stubborn hope that refuses to let go of God entirely.
basic.crossReferences: Genesis 4:10 records Abel's blood crying out from the ground; Hebrews 12:24 says the blood of Jesus speaks a better word than the blood of Abel; Hebrews 7:25 declares Christ always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him, the fulfillment of Job's longed-for advocate.
basic.oneStory: In his darkest language yet, Job reaches for the book's brightest hope so far, a witness and advocate already in heaven. That flash of hope, appearing in the middle of unresolved anguish, anticipates the New Testament's full revelation of Christ as the very advocate and intercessor Job could only long for.

context.literary:
These two chapters are one speech, and it is built as a sequence of turns in who Job is speaking to. He begins with the friends in 16:2 to 5, turns from them to describe God in 16:6 to 17, addresses the earth and heaven in 16:18 to 22, speaks to God directly in 17:1 to 5, turns to the onlookers in 17:6 to 9, and ends by daring the friends to try again in 17:10 to 16. The changing addressee is how the speech carries its emotion. Job cannot settle on anyone who will listen, so he speaks to everyone.

The centre of the first half is a piece of sustained violent imagery. Job pictures God as a wild animal that tears and gnashes, as a wrestler who seizes his neck, as an archer with a target, and as a warrior who storms a breach in a wall. The lines are close to the protest of Lamentations 3:12 to 13, where God bends His bow and sets a man as a target. Job's language is more extreme than that of any friend, and the writer does not soften it.

Then, in 16:18 to 22, the tone shifts within a few lines. Job speaks of blood, of a witness, of an advocate, of tears poured out to God. The hope does not answer the accusations, and it does not cancel them. It sits beside them, and chapter 17 slides back into darkness. The two chapters therefore rehearse the shape of the whole book, protest, reach for a mediator, relapse, and reach again.

There is a small pattern of hands. Job's hands are free of violence, 16:17. He asks for a pledge to be struck, 17:3, which is a gesture made with the hand. And he speaks of the clean hands of the righteous that grow stronger, 17:9. The hand that God has used to break him is set against the hand Job still hopes to keep clean.
context.historical:
Several of the images in these chapters come from the practices of the ancient courtroom and the ancient mourner. Sackcloth sewn over the skin and a horn buried in the dust, 16:15, are acts of grief and humiliation. The horn was a familiar picture for strength and standing, so burying it means Job's dignity has been thrown down into the ground.

The cry that the earth not cover his blood, 16:18, rests on a widely shared belief that blood shed unjustly stayed on the ground as a witness until it was answered. Genesis 4:10 has Abel's blood crying out. Ezekiel 24:7 to 8 speaks of blood left on bare rock, uncovered by dust, so that vengeance would not be forgotten. Isaiah 26:21 promises that the earth will no longer conceal those it has slain. Job speaks as if his own death, when it comes, will be a wrong that needs to be heard, and he asks the earth to hold his cry until then.

The legal scene in 16:19 to 21 and 17:3 draws on the practice of the guarantor. To put up security for another, a man struck hands with the creditor, a gesture that appears in Proverbs 6:1 and 17:18. Proverbs warns against doing it lightly. In Genesis 43:9 and 44:32 Judah takes on exactly that role for his brother Benjamin, promising to bear the guilt if the boy does not return. Job has no human guarantor left, since the friends have failed him, and so he asks God to do it.

Spitting in the face, 17:6, is a mark of the deepest shame. In Numbers 12:14 a father's spitting is enough to bring seven days of disgrace, and Job is spat upon by ordinary people. Becoming a "byword" meant becoming a proverb of misfortune, a fate Deuteronomy 28:37 lists among the curses of covenant breaking. To the first hearers, Job's condition would look like the visible mark of a man judged by God.
context.canonical:
Job's language in chapter 16 is echoed in the Psalms of the afflicted and then, more sharply, in the passion of Christ. The mockers who shake the head, 16:4, appear in Psalm 22:7 and Lamentations 2:15. Those who open their mouths against the sufferer, 16:10, recall Psalm 22:13, and the gnashing of teeth in 16:9 recalls Psalm 35:16 and, at the martyrdom of Stephen, Acts 7:54. The blows to the cheek and the spittle of 16:10 and 17:6 are matched by Isaiah 50:6 and are then carried out on Jesus, Matthew 26:67.

The witness and advocate of 16:19 to 21 belong to a thread that runs through the whole book. Job wished in 9:33 for a mediator who could lay his hand on both parties, and Elihu will speak of a messenger, one in a thousand, who says "I have found his ransom", 33:23 to 24. In 19:25 the thread becomes a redeemer who lives. In the New Testament it becomes a person: Christ 'is interceding for us', Romans 8:34, 'always lives to intercede', Hebrews 7:25, is 'an advocate before the Father', 1 John 2:1, and is the 'one mediator between God and men', 1 Timothy 2:5.

The cry about blood has its answer in Hebrews 12:24, where the sprinkled blood of Jesus speaks a better word than that of Abel. Revelation 6:10 hears the martyrs under the altar crying, 'How long', and their cry does not go unheard.

Finally, Job's despair at the grave, 17:13 to 16, meets its counter in Psalm 16:10 and Psalm 49:15, where the faithful man is not abandoned to Sheol, and in the resurrection hope of 1 Corinthians 15. Chapter 17 asks the question those texts answer.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The writer of Job wants the reader to stand close enough to pain to hear how it actually speaks. He gives Job words that are not tidy, that accuse God of cruelty, and that in the same breath call on God as a witness. The lesson for the first hearers, who were people used to formal prayers and to sages who defended God's ways, was that faith can sound like this, and that it survives being said aloud.

He also wants us to feel what the friends have missed. Job says, in effect, that he could speak their speeches if he stood in their place, 16:4, but he would use his mouth to strengthen rather than to accuse. The speech is a description of what real comfort would be, and a rebuke of anyone who reaches for an answer before they have listened.

Most of all, the writer allows a flash of hope to break through in the middle of accusation, and he does not explain it. Job does not know how a witness in heaven can be reconciled with a God who has broken him. He knows only that he cannot stop appealing. The hearer is invited to see that clinging to God, even against God, is a form of trust, and that faith does not have to wait until all the questions are answered.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
What we have in these chapters is a record of Job's experience and his words, not a set of instructions or a portrait of God. Job's claim that God has handed him to the wicked, 16:11, is how it feels, and the book does not confirm it as a true account of God's character. God will speak, and He will say that Job spoke rightly of Him in the matter of the friends, 42:7, and will also correct Job's ignorance, 38:2. Job himself ends by retracting his words, 42:6.

That means we should not build doctrine from a single line of Job's complaint. The statement that God is his enemy is real as a cry and misleading as a summary of the character of God. What can be taken as instruction is the pattern of the prayer: bring the whole of it, the anger and the fear, before God, and keep appealing beyond the pain.

The chapter also warns against a shallow reading of hope. The advocate of 16:19 does not remove Job's suffering, and the next chapter falls back into gloom. Believers can expect that hope in a hard season may arrive in glimpses and not settle into calm, and that this does not mean the hope was false.

debates.question: Who is the witness and advocate of 16:19 to 21?

views.label: God Himself, appealed to against God
views.case: Job has just described God as his attacker, yet he also says 'Even now my witness is in heaven'. Many readers see this as a daring appeal from God as he seems to be to God as he truly is. It fits verse 20, where Job's tears pour out to God, and verse 21, where he asks that someone plead with God.

views.label: A third party in heaven
views.case: Verse 21 speaks of a man pleading with God as with a neighbour, and 9:33 had asked for a mediator. On this view a separate heavenly figure is in view, like the messenger of 33:23. It respects the language of pleading with God, though the text names no such figure.

views.label: Christ, seen in shadow
views.case: Christian readers have long heard in this the shape of the mediator the New Testament announces, 1 Timothy 2:5. Few would say Job knew this. The claim is that the writer and the Spirit behind him were shaping a longing the gospel would answer.

debates.bearing: The text does not settle the identity, and it does not need to. What matters is the direction of Job's reach: past his experience of God's silence toward a God who will speak for him. That direction is the one the gospel fills in.

debates.question: What does Job mean when he asks God to be his guarantor in 17:3?

views.label: A last legal move
views.case: Job asks God to put down the pledge that a court would require, since no one else will vouch for him. The verse then works as an argument: God alone can safely guarantee, and He alone has closed the friends' minds, verse 4.

views.label: A prayer that God would stand surety against Himself
views.case: Some read it as a striking paradox: the opponent is asked to be the guarantor. This is the same tension as the witness in heaven, and it treats the verse as another step in the appeal from God to God.

views.label: A rhetorical challenge
views.case: A few take the verse as bitter irony, a demand that God prove His case or step aside. The tone of 17:1 to 2 would support that.

debates.bearing: On any of these readings, Job admits he cannot rescue himself and that only God is able to. The New Testament calls Jesus the guarantee of a better covenant, Hebrews 7:22, and shows that God has in fact provided the pledge that Job could only request.

study.originalLanguages:
In 16:2 Job calls his friends "miserable comforters". The Hebrew sets the ordinary word for comfort beside amal, the word for trouble or toil. It is the word Eliphaz used when he said that man is born to trouble, 5:7, and that the wicked conceive trouble, 15:35. Job throws it back: they are comforters who bring only trouble. The bite of the phrase is in the repetition.

The verb "to plead" in 16:21 is from the root yakach, which means to argue a case, to set out what is right, or to reprove. The same root gives the "mediator" of 9:33 and Job's wish in 13:3 to argue his case before God. So the wish of 16:21, that a man might plead with God as with his neighbour, is the third time in the book that Job asks for someone to stand between himself and God in a court of argument. It is a settled longing, not a passing thought.

In 17:3 the idiom for "guarantor" is the handclasp of surety. The Hebrew asks, in effect, who else will strike hands for me. The same gesture appears in Proverbs 6:1, and the noun for pledge is related to the verb Judah uses in Genesis 43:9 when he promises to be answerable for Benjamin. Job wants a guarantor who will take responsibility for his standing, and he sees that only God is able.

The word "hands" recurs with a moral point. In 16:17 Job says his hands are free of violence, chamas, a word Isaiah 53:9 uses when it says the servant had done no violence. In 17:9 the one with clean hands grows stronger. The book keeps a clear line between what Job's hands have done and what was done to him.

In 17:14 Job says to "corruption", "You are my father", and to the worm, "My mother". The word for corruption can also mean a pit, and Psalm 16:10 uses it when it says God will not let His Holy One see decay. Job is claiming kinship with the very place the Psalm says God will not abandon a faithful man to. That link makes Job's despair and the Psalm's confidence two sides of a single word.

Finally, the word for hope in 17:15 is also used for a cord. The scarlet cord Rahab ties in her window, Joshua 2:18, is called by this word. Hope in this language is something you hold on to, and Job asks who can see any cord left to hold.

typology.type: The one struck and spat upon, 16:10 and 17:6
typology.fulfillment: Job is struck on the cheek, made a byword, and spat upon in the face. Isaiah's servant offers his back to those who strike and does not hide his face from scorn and spittle, Isaiah 50:6, and Jesus receives exactly this from the soldiers and the council, Matthew 26:67 and 27:26. The correspondence is a pattern of the righteous man treated as a criminal. It escalates in Christ because His suffering is chosen and redemptive, Mark 10:45. It falls short at one point: Job protests his innocence and asks why, while Jesus goes to the cross knowing what it is for.

Job insists that his hands are free of violence, chamas. Isaiah 53:9 says the servant was assigned a grave with the wicked 'although He had done no violence'. Job foreshadows the innocent sufferer, and Christ completes the picture, since 1 Peter 2:22 says He committed no sin and no deceit was found in His mouth. The type is limited: Job's claim is relative, made against the friends' charges and not before God's perfect standard, while Christ's innocence is absolute, which is why His death can be for others, 1 Peter 3:18.

typology.type: The witness and advocate on high, 16:19
typology.fulfillment: Job's longing for a heavenly witness anticipates the risen Christ, who has entered 'heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God', Hebrews 9:24. The correspondence is between a sufferer's need for a heavenly ally and the priest who lives to intercede, Hebrews 7:25. It escalates because Job asked for someone to plead with God, while Jesus is at once God and man, and His plea is grounded in His own blood, Hebrews 9:12. The type falls short in that Job did not know who his witness was.

typology.type: The blood that must not be covered, 16:18
typology.fulfillment: Abel's blood cried from the ground, Genesis 4:10, and Job asks that his cry not be silenced. Hebrews 12:24 says the blood of Jesus 'speaks a better word than the blood of Abel'. The blood of Abel called for justice; the blood of Christ secures mercy, 1 Peter 1:19. Job's blood, if shed, would have witnessed to an unrighted wrong. Christ's blood witnesses to a wrong that has been answered, and a debt that has been paid.

study.christ:
The chapters lead to Christ first by the shape of the suffering. Job is mocked, struck across the face, spat upon and turned into a proverb, and the New Testament records every one of these things done to Jesus. He is spat on and slapped, Matthew 26:67, and He is mocked by those who shake their heads, Matthew 27:39. The Psalms of the afflicted that carry these images, Psalm 22 above all, are the words He prays on the cross. Job is not the Messiah, and his sufferings are not a prediction of the passion. But the innocent man under the hand of God and the crowd is a shape the Bible lets us see again in full.

They lead to Christ by longing. Job cries, 'Oh, that a man might plead with God as he pleads with his neighbor!', 16:21. The Bible's answer is a man who is God: 'there is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus', 1 Timothy 2:5. Job asked for a witness on high; the risen Christ 'entered heaven itself, now to appear on our behalf in the presence of God', Hebrews 9:24. Job asked for a guarantor; Jesus 'has become the guarantee of a better covenant', Hebrews 7:22. The Hebrew idiom of striking hands is answered by nail-pierced ones.

They lead to Christ by the contrast between the accuser and the advocate. Job is besieged by voices that accuse him, and the New Testament names the accuser who accuses the brothers day and night before God, Revelation 12:10. Against that voice stands Christ, who lives to intercede, Romans 8:34, and, as John puts it, is 'an advocate before the Father', 1 John 2:1. Job asked for someone to speak against the accusations, and the gospel gives the person who speaks and who has paid.

They lead to Christ through the grave. Job says of the pit, 'You are my father', and asks where his hope is, 17:14 to 15. Psalm 16:10 says God will not let His Holy One see decay, and Peter preaches that Jesus is that Holy One, Acts 2:27 to 31. The question that Job asks, where then is hope, is answered by an empty tomb, 1 Corinthians 15:20.

The guard against forced reading is that Job did not know any of this. The texts that fulfil his longing come from later. But they fulfil it without strain, because the longing was real and was given by the same Spirit who inspired the book.
study.god:
The God of these chapters is felt as an assailant. Job uses the verbs of violence for Him: He tears, gnashes, seizes, shatters, pierces, and spills. The Bible allows this, and the fact that Scripture keeps such speech in its canon tells us something about God: He does not need to be defended by softened language. He can be addressed in the worst terms of a person's experience.

Yet the same God is the one Job appeals to. Job's tears are poured out 'to God', 16:20, and his witness is in heaven, 16:19. The tension is not ironed out. It is the pressure of the book: the God who seems to be Job's enemy is the only one who can be his advocate. That says something about the nature of faith. When God is hidden, the believer cannot go elsewhere. Peter's answer, 'Lord, to whom would we go?', John 6:68, is already the logic of Job.

The chapters also show God's silence as a matter of real hurt. In 16:6 to 8 Job cannot find relief in speaking or holding back, and in 17:2 to 3 he sees mockers around him and no answer from heaven. Nothing in these chapters gives a reason. The book will supply, in the end, not a reason but a presence, Job 42:5. The doctrine is that God does not always explain, and that He is still worth appealing to.

The chapter holds another truth about God: He is the one who takes up the cause of the wronged. Job's belief that a witness in heaven exists, and that blood does not disappear from the record, depends on a God who sees. Genesis 4:10 shows God hearing Abel's blood, and Revelation 6:10 shows Him hearing the martyrs. Job trusts, even while suffering, that the courtroom of heaven is not empty.

Finally, God is, in the ordering of the gospel, both the one who is offended and the one who provides the guarantee. Job's daring request that God be his own guarantor, 17:3, is answered in the sending of the Son, 'He who did not spare His own Son but gave Him up for us all', Romans 8:32. For worship, the chapters teach honest prayer. They give words to people who do not have any, and they show that the way through darkness is to keep speaking to God, and to ask for the witness, the advocate and the guarantor that only He can supply.

crossReferences.note: Job's earlier wish for a mediator who could lay his hand on both God and himself. Chapter 16 sharpens it: the witness is now said to exist, and the request is to plead with God as a man does with his neighbour. Reading the two together shows how a longing grows across the book.

Abel's blood cries out from the ground, and God hears it. Job's request that the earth not cover his blood assumes that story: blood shed wrongly does not vanish, and the ground itself is a witness. It is why the hope of 16:18 is more than sentiment.

The bow bent, the target set, the arrows piercing the kidneys. The language of 16:12 to 13 is almost the same, which shows that Job's most extreme speech belongs to a recognised tradition of lament that Scripture itself preserves and later uses for the whole people.

Mockers shake their heads and open their mouths against the sufferer like lions. Job's picture of the mocking crowd in 16:4 and 16:10 shares its images. The Psalm is the one Jesus prays on the cross, so the mockery Job describes becomes part of the pattern of the righteous sufferer.

The servant offers his cheeks to those who strike and does not hide from spittle. Job is struck on the cheek and spat upon, and does not hide his misery. The Servant Song shows what Job could not know: the suffering of the innocent can be embraced and can be redemptive.

Jesus is the guarantee of a better covenant and lives always to intercede. Job's request for a guarantor in 17:3 and an advocate in 16:19 is answered here. The passage also explains why Job's hope was not misplaced: there is such a person, and He is able to save completely.

'Who will bring any charge against God's elect? It is God who justifies.' Paul answers the accuser's questions with the advocate's intercession. This is the resolution Job could only long for, and it shows that the courtroom language of the book was always meant to be answered in Christ.

God will not abandon the soul to Sheol or let His Holy One see decay. Job calls decay his father and Sheol his home, and asks where hope is. The Psalm answers the question Job raises, and Peter applies it to Jesus in Acts 2:27.

Elihu speaks of a messenger, one mediator in a thousand, who says 'I have found his ransom'. It carries Job's longing for a mediator further, and connects the advocate with ransom. It shows the theme of an intermediary is developed across several speakers in the book.

The souls of the martyrs cry out from beneath the altar for justice, and their cry is heard. Job's request that his cry never be laid to rest has this large echo: the blood of the wronged does not go unanswered in God's ordering of history.

study.oneStory:
The two chapters sit at a hinge in the story of the whole Bible: a person in pain, unable to find a mediator, reaching past his experience for someone who will speak for him. From Genesis onward the story has been about a breach between God and humanity, Genesis 3, and about the need for a way across it. In Job that need is felt by one man, in one place, with unusual honesty.

What the chapters answer from before is the question of what a sufferer may say to God. Genesis 4 shows a righteous man dead and his blood crying out. The Psalms show the language of lament. Job carries that language to its limit: God appears as the attacker, the friends as false comforters, and the grave as the only future. The Bible does not censor him. It places him on the road toward the answer, and it treats his hardest words as part of a faithful person's prayer.

What the chapters set up is a line of longing that the rest of the story pursues. Job asks for a witness, an advocate and a guarantor. The prophets speak of a servant who bears griefs, Isaiah 53:4. The letter to the Hebrews describes a high priest who is able to sympathise, who has entered heaven, and who lives to intercede, Hebrews 4:15 and 7:25. What Job could name only as a hope is named there as a person and a work.

The chapters also show that the answer does not remove all pain at once. Job is not delivered in chapter 16. The witness is in heaven while he is still on the ground. That is the position of every believer between the cross and the return of Christ: the advocate is real and active, and the world is still broken. Paul says creation groans, and we groan with it, Romans 8:22 to 23.

The story ends where Job's hope was aimed. In the new creation the accuser is thrown down, Revelation 12:10, and the one who seemed to be the enemy is seen face to face as the friend of the ransomed. The question of 17:15, where then is my hope, is answered by a city in which God will wipe away every tear, Revelation 21:4, and the earth no longer covers its dead, Isaiah 26:19 and 21.

sermon.title: Why Suffering?
sermon.why: Begg preaches directly on Job 16:7-17, the heart of Job's description of feeling personally assailed by God, addressing the raw honesty of this passage's language about suffering at God's own hand.

quiz.q: What sudden hope does Job voice in the middle of his darkest complaint (16:18-19)?

options.text: That his witness is already in heaven and his advocate is on high, even while he describes feeling personally torn apart by God.
options.note: This flash of hope appears immediately after Job's most violent language about God's assault against him, without waiting for his anguish to be resolved first.

options.text: That heaven itself already holds testimony to the truth of his innocence, even though his friends have become his scoffers.
options.note: A true summary of Job's hope, though less precise than his exact naming of a witness and advocate already present on high.

options.text: That he has finally discovered his hidden sin.
options.note: Job's hope here concerns vindication of his innocence through a heavenly witness, not the discovery of hidden guilt.

options.text: That his friends will finally admit he is right.
options.note: Job's hope here is directed toward heaven, not toward his friends, whom he calls scoffers in the very next verse.

quiz.q: What image does Job use to describe how he feels God has treated him in chapter 16?

options.text: Like a target for archers, seized by the throat and crushed by a mighty warrior.
options.note: Verses 12-14 use this vivid, violent imagery of assault to describe Job's experience of suffering at what he perceives as God's own hand.

options.text: Like an enemy whose anger tears and opposes him, gnashing its teeth against him.
options.note: A true, related image from earlier in the same chapter, though less vivid than the specific archer and warrior imagery of verses 12-14.

options.text: Like a physician carefully treating a wound.
options.note: Job's language describes wounds being inflicted, wound upon wound, rather than a physician's careful healing.

options.text: Like a shepherd gently guiding his flock.
options.note: This is the opposite of the violent, assaultive imagery Job actually uses in this chapter.

quiz.q: Why is the phrase 'do not cover my blood' (16:18) significant?

options.text: It echoes Abel's blood crying out from the ground in Genesis 4:10, showing Job wants his suffering to be heard and acknowledged, not silenced or forgotten.
options.note: This deliberate echo connects Job's cry to one of the earliest biblical images of an unheard, unavenged wrong crying out for acknowledgment.

options.text: It shows Job wants his cry for help to never be laid to rest or forgotten.
options.note: Correctly captures Job's basic wish, though less precise than identifying the specific echo of Abel's blood from Genesis 4:10.

options.text: It has no connection to any other part of Scripture.
options.note: The connection to Genesis 4:10's account of Abel's blood is a widely recognized biblical echo.

options.text: It refers to a literal wound Job wants treated by a physician.
options.note: The phrase is figurative, about his cry for justice being heard, not a request for medical treatment.

quiz.q: How does chapter 17 close, and what does that reveal about Job's state?

options.text: With an unresolved question, where then is my hope, showing that even in apparent despair Job has not entirely stopped asking or hoping.
options.note: The very act of continuing to ask about hope, rather than falling silent, suggests hope persists even in this dark closing passage.

options.text: With Job picturing Sheol as his likely home, yet still asking whether any hope could go down there with him.
options.note: A true description of the chapter's final images, though less precise than naming the unresolved question itself as the closing note.

options.text: With a full explanation from God about the reason for Job's suffering.
options.note: God does not speak until much later in the book, chapters 38 to 41; no explanation is given here.

options.text: With a confident declaration that his suffering is now over.
options.note: The chapter closes in continued lament and unresolved questioning, not confident resolution.

quiz.q: How does Job's longing for a witness and advocate in heaven connect to the New Testament?

options.text: It anticipates Christ's ongoing intercession for His people, since Hebrews 7:25 says He always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him.
options.note: This connection presents Job's hope as a genuine anticipation of the New Testament's fuller revelation of Christ's mediatorial and intercessory role.

options.text: It points toward a heavenly figure who represents believers before God, an idea the New Testament develops much further.
options.note: Correct in its general direction, though less precise than naming Hebrews 7:25's specific answer of Christ's continual intercession.

options.text: It refers only to Job's own future vindication in this life.
options.note: While Job is restored later in the book, this specific image of a witness and advocate in heaven points to something larger than earthly restoration, ultimately fulfilled in Christ's heavenly intercession.

options.text: It has no meaningful connection to later biblical revelation.
options.note: The language of an advocate and witness in heaven closely anticipates Christ's intercessory role as described in Hebrews.

questions: Right in the middle of his darkest complaint, Job reaches for hope in a heavenly witness. Has hope ever surprised you in the middle of grief, before your circumstances had actually changed?

Job describes feeling personally targeted and torn apart, yet still trusts someone in heaven knows the truth of his case. Where do you need to trust that God, or someone, sees the truth of your situation even when it feels like no one around you does?
Job's cry, do not cover my blood, is a plea to be heard rather than silenced or forgotten. What pain in your own life have you tried to bury rather than bring honestly into the light?

Job longs for an advocate who could plead his case with God, a longing the New Testament says is answered in Christ's ongoing intercession. How does knowing Christ intercedes for you change how you pray about something you cannot resolve on your own?
This passage ends without full resolution, still asking where hope can be found. What helps you keep asking, rather than giving up entirely, when your own hope feels nearly exhausted?

translationNotes.note: Do not cover my blood deliberately echoes the language of Genesis 4:10, where Abel's blood cries out from the ground, casting Job's suffering as an unheard wrong crying out for acknowledgment and justice.

Advocate renders sahed, a rare term appearing only here in the Hebrew Bible, likely related to an Aramaic root for witness; paired with ed, witness, in the same verse, it intensifies Job's sudden hope of heavenly vindication.
Guarantor renders a legal term for someone who posts security or surety on another's behalf, continuing the book's recurring legal imagery of Job seeking someone to stand as his advocate before God.
